analysis.one_liner: Bars licensed gun dealers from selling more than one handgun to the same person within a month.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in the Senate in February 1999, referred to the Judiciary Committee, and never received a committee hearing, a floor vote, or became law.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make it a federal crime for a licensed gun dealer to sell two or more handguns to an unlicensed buyer within any 30-day period, and for an unlicensed person to buy that many handguns in that window. It would also raise the penalty for lying on federal firearm purchase paperwork from one year to five years, extend how long certain background-check records must be kept before destruction, and expand the legal definition of a gun dealer to cover anyone who resells more than one handgun a month.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people in communities affected by gun violence, especially in cities where traffickers buy cheap handguns in bulk in states with weak rules and resell them illegally in stricter states. Police also benefit from reduced street trafficking.

how_it_helps.text: Cuts off the most common bulk-buying method used by gun traffickers: purchasing several handguns at once from a licensed dealer, then reselling them illegally on the street.
Raises the penalty for knowingly making false statements in connection with firearm purchases from one year to five years, increasing the deterrent against straw purchases.
Extends record-retention deadlines for background-check records from 20 business days to 35 calendar days, giving investigators more time to trace guns used in crimes.

Broadens the definition of someone 'engaged in the business' of selling firearms to include anyone reselling more than one handgun per month to non-dealers, closing a loophole used by high-volume unlicensed sellers.

analysis.who_pays: Law-abiding gun buyers who want to purchase more than one handgun in a month face new federal restrictions and potential criminal penalties, and licensed dealers face compliance burdens, lost sales volume, and new legal exposure.
analysis.who_pays_short: Licensed gun dealers and repeat buyers

drawbacks.text: Law-abiding collectors and buyers who want more than one handgun in a month — for example, buying gifts or multiple firearms at once — would be barred or face federal penalty, a genuine restriction on legal conduct.
Licensed dealers bear the cost of refusing repeat sales and risk criminal liability, while the bill does not change how guns acquired before the rule change are transferred between individuals.
The bill does not address the large existing stock of guns already in circulation, so it targets future trafficking only and would take time to affect street-level supply.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is reducing bulk purchases that fuel illegal gun trafficking, a real problem for city residents and police. The cost is a new federal restriction on some legal purchases and added compliance for dealers. The trade-off is narrow in scope — one handgun per month is still allowed — but it is a real new limit on lawful conduct, and the bill's narrow focus leaves existing gun stocks untouched.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate Judiciary Committee never acted on the bill after its referral in February 1999, so it died at the end of the 106th Congress without a hearing, a markup, or any vote.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced by Senator Frank Lautenberg with 11 cosponsors on February 10, 1999, and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee.
No further action was recorded after the referral; the bill never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote, and expired when the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Gun trafficking channels that rely on bulk purchases at licensed dealers were left untouched, and licensed dealers retained the ability to sell multiple handguns to the same buyer within a month.

for.name: Sen. Frank Lautenberg
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to restrict bulk handgun sales.

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over firearms legislation
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral in February 1999 and took no action, letting it die without a hearing or vote.

sides.party_line_note: All 11 cosponsors were Democrats, and no Republican support is recorded in the bill's history or sponsor list.

industries.note: Dealers would lose the ability to sell multiple handguns to the same buyer within a month and would face new criminal liability for violations, cutting into sales volume and compliance costs rise.
People reselling more than one handgun per month would fall under the federal dealer licensing and regulatory requirements, ending their unregulated status.
